title: Big Tech earnings this week will put the AI capex thesis on trial
subtitle: Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta report Wednesday; Amazon and Apple follow Thursday. With Meta still in negative free cash flow and the Nasdaq jittery, the week decides whether the roughly $700 billion the four hyperscalers plan to spend in 2026 can be defended out loud.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta report Q3 2026 results after the close on Wednesday, October 28. Amazon and Apple follow on Thursday. The headline numbers are already set: Alphabet lifted its 2026 capex guidance to $195–$205 billion over the summer, Microsoft management has flagged roughly $190 billion for the year, and the combined hyperscaler figure for 2026 sits near $700 billion by analyst estimates. The question this week is not whether that spending happened — it did — but whether the AI revenue being counted against it is tracking fast enough to justify it. Microsoft said in April its AI business crossed a $37 billion annual run rate; Google Cloud backlog hit $514 billion by end of June on 82% year-on-year growth. Those are the baselines investors will mark against.

The pressure sharpened last quarter. Meta drifted into negative free cash flow and the stock fell hard on raised capex guidance, with Reuters framing it as a signal that even trillion-dollar firms can out-spend their own cash generation if AI buildout accelerates faster than monetization. Since then the Nasdaq has sold off multiple times on AI-cost concerns, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent — in a closed-door exchange reported by the Financial Times on October 22 — argued the sector does not pose 'systemic' risk even as he acknowledged firms have not explained the public benefit well. Four Democratic senators have asked the Financial Stability Oversight Council to probe the special-purpose-vehicle financing hyperscalers are using to keep data-center debt off balance sheets.

What's actually at stake this week is the shape of the narrative, not the numbers. If Google Cloud growth accelerates and Microsoft's AI run rate reaccelerates with gross margins stabilizing, the capex story holds and the hyperscalers continue to look like beneficiaries of a durable platform shift. If AWS growth slips, if Microsoft's capital intensity keeps rising while gross margin keeps falling, or if Meta's guidance surprises higher again without a corresponding revenue path, the market will have real ammunition for a sharper repricing. Oracle's AI World conference running through Wednesday adds a side signal — Oracle's cloud-and-AI commentary this week has historically moved the sector.

A note for learners: capex-to-revenue is the metric to watch, not absolute spending. $200 billion a year is a huge number in isolation and a reasonable one if the backlog it is building off is $500 billion and growing 80%. If you are learning to read financial statements, use this week to practice: pull the 10-Qs when they land, divide capital expenditures by revenue for each hyperscaler, compare the trend across quarters, and ask whether the resulting ratio looks like a durable platform or like a one-way bet on a model generation that could age quickly.
